oneSentence: A United Nations-led process for bringing governments and other relevant actors together to discuss shared approaches for managing AI across borders.
plainExplanation:
This term refers to a specific United Nations discussion process about how AI should be governed. Governance means the rules, institutions, practices and oversight used to guide how AI is developed and used. “Global” matters because AI systems, companies, data flows and technical standards often cross borders.

Different countries, UN bodies, experts, companies and civil society groups can bring concerns, evidence and proposals. Topics may include safety, human rights, development, interoperability, accountability and capacity-building, which means helping countries build the skills and systems they need.

Meetings, consultations and reports help participants compare priorities and identify common ground. The dialogue may inform later recommendations, principles, resolutions or normative instruments. Normative instruments are formally adopted texts that set shared principles, expectations or guidance.

The dialogue does not itself create a binding rule. Its outputs may include shared language, clearer problem definitions, areas of agreement and a basis for later action in other forums. It is a specific discussion process, not one document, regulation or expert body.

everydayAnalogy.title: Several schools discussing rules for a shared messaging app
everydayAnalogy.story: Several schools use the same messaging app, but each has different rules and concerns. Teachers want reliable moderation, students want privacy, parents want clear safeguards and some schools need better language and accessibility support. They meet to compare approaches, hear technical advice and identify where they agree. They also record questions they cannot yet settle. The discussion does not impose one rulebook on every school, but it can shape later decisions, shared guidance and practical support.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A library network is much smaller and simpler than global AI governance. In real international dialogue, participants may have conflicting legal systems, strategic interests and unequal technical capacity. Also, the global dialogue can influence later UN texts, standards and national policies, while the library meeting mainly affects one service.

visual.title: How a global dialogue on AI governance moves from concerns to shared next steps
visual.learningObjective: Show that the dialogue is a process: issues are raised, discussed across groups, and may lead to shared language or later policy work, not instant global rules.
visual.description: A left-to-right step diagram with five boxes. Read from concerns entering the process to possible outputs. Arrows show that each step builds on the previous one, but the final box lists several possible outcomes rather than a single result.

steps.label: 1. Issues raised
steps.explanation: Countries and other participants bring problems, evidence and priorities such as safety, inclusion, development or accountability.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with small input icons: speech bubbles, a document, a shield and a globe. Label inputs from governments, experts, industry and civil society.

steps.label: 2. Dialogue organised
steps.explanation: The UN or another agreed forum structures meetings, consultations or reports so participants can compare views.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with a calendar and meeting table. Add a small label: consultations, meetings, reports.

steps.label: 3. Differences examined
steps.explanation: Participants identify where views align and where they differ, including legal, technical and development concerns.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with two overlapping circles and coloured notes marked agreement and difference.

steps.label: 4. Common ground shaped
steps.explanation: Shared terms, principles or options are drafted, even if some issues remain unsettled.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with a draft document and highlighted lines. Add a small note: not necessarily binding.

steps.label: 5. Next steps
steps.explanation: The process may inform resolutions, standards, capacity-building or later negotiations in other forums.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final box splitting into three small outputs: policy text, standards checklist and training/capacity icon.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each step to reveal a short example of what might happen there, with the arrow path highlighted.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains the process behind a global dialogue on AI governance in five steps. First, participants such as governments, experts, companies and civil society bring concerns and evidence about AI. Second, an international forum organises meetings, consultations or reports. Third, participants compare positions and identify both agreements and disagreements. Fourth, they draft shared language, principles or options, though these may not be binding. Fifth, the dialogue may feed into later outputs such as resolutions, standards work or capacity-building. The main message is that the dialogue is a staged process that helps build common ground rather than an instant world law.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-step horizontal diagram with numbered boxes and arrows. Each box includes a short label and one icon. Expanded text for each step appears below the diagram instead of using hover or animation.

workedExample.scenario: A United Nations-led consultation examines how different jurisdictions approach transparency and human oversight for high-impact AI systems.
workedExample.input: Member States provide positions, experts present evidence, stakeholders submit written views and the Secretariat prepares a background note identifying recurring questions.
process: The Secretariat organises the inputs by issue and circulates an agenda that reflects both frequently raised concerns and proposals requiring further discussion.
During consultations, participants identify areas of convergence, including the value of testing, documentation and accessible capacity-building.
They also record unresolved questions, such as when voluntary guidance may be sufficient and when binding requirements may be considered.
A meeting report sets out the convergences, disagreements and possible follow-up, without treating every intervention as an agreed conclusion.
workedExample.result: The dialogue does not itself create one global AI law. It gives governments and other participants a clearer basis for political guidance, standards work, capacity-building or later negotiations in the appropriate forums.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A desk officer at Headquarters is clearing talking points for afternoon informals on AI governance. The front office needs one paragraph that explains what a global dialogue can produce without accidentally turning a consultation into a treaty.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The term helps the officer distinguish the dialogue's agenda-setting role from later decision-making. Meetings and reports can map convergence, preserve disagreements and identify possible cooperation, while resolutions, standards or negotiations proceed through their own forums.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not present a chair's summary or Secretariat note as an agreed Member State position. Restricted submissions and negotiating instructions must not be entered into an external AI tool, because doing so could disclose positions that were not intended for circulation.

whyItMatters: A non-specialist may hear this term in news, UN documents or policy debates and assume it means a single global law is coming. It instead names a structured United Nations process for comparing risks, values and options. The discussions can shape whose concerns count, which problems get priority, and whether smaller or lower-capacity countries can influence later work. They can also help participants consider whether future approaches will work across borders or clash with each other.
whereYouMayHearIt: Informals on a General Assembly text concerning AI governance
A Secretariat briefing before Member State consultations
A side event on cross-border approaches to AI oversight
A permanent mission's preparation meeting before a first reading

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It means the world has already agreed on one set of AI rules.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A dialogue is a process for discussion and coordination. It may lead to shared principles or later negotiations, but it does not by itself create one binding global rulebook.

Governments are central in intergovernmental settings, but many discussions also involve experts, civil society, companies and technical bodies. Exactly who participates depends on the forum and mandate.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It is the same thing as the UN scientific panel on AI.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The scientific panel is a specific body focused on evidence and analysis. The global dialogue is broader and refers to the wider international discussion and coordination process around AI governance.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: It is a United Nations process where countries and other relevant actors discuss how AI should be guided and overseen across borders.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In more precise terms, this is a United Nations process for agenda-setting and consultation on AI governance across jurisdictions. Inputs can include Member State positions, expert evidence, stakeholder submissions and Secretariat support. Through meetings and reports, participants identify convergences, disagreements and possible areas for cooperation. The dialogue may inform political guidance, resolutions, standards work, capacity-building priorities or later negotiations in other forums. It does not itself imply a binding treaty, a single institution or consensus on all substantive issues.

keyTakeaway: It is a process for finding common ground and mapping disagreements on AI governance across jurisdictions, not a single meeting, law or negotiating body.

quickCheck.question: Which description best fits a global dialogue on AI governance?
options: A process where countries and other relevant actors discuss shared approaches to AI across borders
A binding global treaty that automatically applies to every AI system
A single expert panel that alone writes all international AI rules
A technical method for training AI models on data from many countries
quickCheck.explanation: The first option describes a discussion and coordination process. A treaty is binding, a panel is a separate body, and model training is a technical activity.

contested: The exact scope of this phrase can vary. Some people use it narrowly for UN-linked follow-up to recent digital cooperation processes, while others use it more broadly for international AI governance discussions across many forums.

issues.problem: The page treats the capitalised term as the wider international conversation rather than a specific United Nations process. It also says negotiations occur within the dialogue, which wrongly suggests a negotiating function. Its shortened definition of a normative instrument omits formal adoption and therefore blurs that distinct term.
issues.fix: Define it consistently as a specific United Nations discussion process. Replace negotiations with comparison of positions and possible follow-up in other forums. Describe normative instruments as formally adopted texts that set principles, expectations or guidance.

issues.problem: “Shared terms, principles or options are drafted” presents the dialogue as a drafting or negotiating body. A discussion process may identify common ground without itself drafting an agreed instrument.
issues.fix: Possible shared terms, principles or options are identified, even if some issues remain unsettled.

issues.problem: “Usually it means” again presents the named term as a generic label for any structured international effort. That fails to distinguish the specific United Nations process from the wider field of multilateral AI governance.
issues.fix: A non-specialist may hear this term in news, UN documents or policy debates and assume it means a single global law is coming. It instead names a structured United Nations process for comparing risks, values and options. The discussions can shape whose concerns count, which problems get priority, and whether smaller or lower-capacity countries can influence later work. They can also help participants consider whether future approaches will work across borders or clash with each other.

issues.problem: The correction calls the scientific panel an existing “specific body”, contradicting the supplied distinct entry, which describes it as proposed.
issues.fix: The proposed scientific panel would focus on evidence and analysis. The global dialogue is a separate discussion and coordination process involving governments and other relevant actors.

issues.problem: Calling it “the international conversation” is too broad. Many international conversations about AI fall outside this named United Nations process.
issues.fix: It is a United Nations process where countries and other relevant actors discuss how AI should be guided and overseen across borders.

issues.problem: “A UN-linked or multilateral process” wrongly expands the named term to cover unspecified multilateral processes. “Negotiations” and “possible norm-shaping” also blur the dialogue with processes that draft or adopt normative instruments.
issues.fix: In more precise terms, this is a United Nations process for agenda-setting and consultation on AI governance across jurisdictions. Inputs can include Member State positions, expert evidence, stakeholder submissions and Secretariat support. Through meetings and reports, participants identify convergences, disagreements and possible areas for cooperation. The dialogue may inform political guidance, resolutions, standards work, capacity-building priorities or later negotiations in other forums. It does not itself imply a binding treaty, a single institution or consensus on all substantive issues.

issues.problem: “The international process” remains broad enough to imply that all international AI governance discussions form part of this named dialogue.
issues.fix: Think of it as a United Nations process for building common ground on AI governance, not as a single law, meeting or expert panel.

issues.problem: The explanation says the dialogue can inform later panels. The supplied definition gives the opposite relevant relationship: the proposed scientific panel would provide evidence for global discussions. The claim about later panels is unsupported and misleading.
issues.fix: The first option describes a discussion and coordination process. A treaty is binding, a panel is a separate body, and model training is a technical activity.

issues.problem: Option 0 is the only defensible answer, but the other three options are caricatures. “Automatically applies to every AI system”, “alone writes all international AI rules” and a model-training method can be rejected without understanding the term.
issues.fix: Replace the distractors with plausible confusions, such as a scientific advisory body, a process for adopting binding regulations, and a formally adopted text setting shared expectations.
